questions.question: What do a Go slice's length and capacity mean?
questions.title: Go slice internals: length, capacity, and backing array
questions.direct_answer: A Go slice is a view over part of an underlying array. Its length, returned by `len(s)`, is the number of elements currently accessible by index. Its capacity, returned by `cap(s)`, is the largest length the slice can reach by reslicing from its current starting position without changing storage. Capacity does not make an index legal; an index must be below length. An append that fits may reuse the backing array, while an append that exceeds capacity returns a slice using new storage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether length, capacity, and the backing array are distinguished.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Indexing up to capacity without first extending the slice length.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Capacity describes reslicing room from the current start; it does not guarantee future append behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A slice describes a window over an underlying array rather than owning a fixed array value.
`len(s)` is the number of elements currently accessible through indexes `0` to `len(s)-1`.
`cap(s)` is the reslicing room from the slice's current start to its capacity limit.
Capacity permits reslicing; it does not permit indexing beyond the current length.
Append may reuse the array within capacity or return a slice backed by new storage.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A slice is a small Go value that describes a contiguous window over an underlying array. Its observable state includes where the window begins, how many elements are currently visible, and how far that window may extend. Assigning or subslicing normally copies this description, not the elements.

`len(s)` is the number of elements in the visible window. Valid indexes run from `0` through `len(s)-1`. Even if extra backing-array storage exists, `s[len(s)]` is out of range until the slice is extended or appended.

`cap(s)` is the largest length that this slice can reach by reslicing from its current start without crossing its capacity limit. With `base := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}` and `s := base[1:3]`, the slice has length two and capacity four.

The operation `s = s[:4]` is valid in that example because four is within capacity. Afterward, length is four and all four elements are indexable. Capacity was permission to extend the view; it was not permission to read `s[3]` before the reslice.

An append that fits within available capacity may reuse the same backing array, so aliases can observe its writes. When the result needs more capacity, `append` obtains storage and returns an updated slice. Always keep the returned slice, and do not depend on a particular growth amount.

sections.title: The visible window and its remaining room
sections.content:
A slice does not contain its elements inline in the way an array value does. It describes access to a range of an underlying array. The length records how much of that range is currently visible. The capacity records how far the visible range may be extended from the same starting position before crossing its limit.

Starting position matters. If a five-element slice is cut with `base[1:3]`, the result begins at the second array element. Its length is two, but its capacity can extend only from that new start to the end available through the source. The element before the start is not part of its capacity.

Indexing and reslicing ask different questions. Indexing requires an index below the current length. Reslicing may increase the length up to capacity and exposes values already present in the backing array. Those values are often zero after `make`, but capacity alone does not say they are meaningful application data.

Capacity also influences append. An append may reuse spare room, which can make writes visible through another slice sharing the array. Once more room is required, append returns a slice using new storage. Go does not promise a fixed capacity-growth formula, so programs should reason about ownership and retain append's returned slice rather than predict its size.

sections.title: One slice window over one backing array
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Backing array - 10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
  A --> B[Slice starts at backing index 1]
  B --> C[len 2 - 20 and 30 visible]
  C --> D[cap 4 - may reslice through 50]
```
Length marks the visible window; capacity marks the remaining window from the same start.

sections.title: Observe length, capacity, and reslicing
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	base := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
	s := base[1:3]
	fmt.Println(s, len(s), cap(s))

	s = s[:4]
	fmt.Println(s, len(s), cap(s))
}
```

questions.question: Which slice expressions are valid in Go?
questions.title: Valid slice bounds and reslicing rules in Go
questions.direct_answer: A two-index slice expression `a[low:high]` uses a half-open range: `low` is included and `high` is excluded, so the result length is `high-low`. For a slice, explicit bounds may reslice up to capacity, but ordinary indexing is still limited by current length. The bounds must be ordered and within the allowed limit. A constant-invalid expression fails to compile; invalid bounds calculated at run time panic. Reslicing exposes existing backing-array elements—it does not prove that they contain meaningful application data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether indexing limits and reslicing limits are kept separate.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming capacity alone makes an index accessible.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Extending length exposes allocated elements; it does not validate that they contain meaningful data.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `a[low:high]` includes `low`, excludes `high`, and has length `high-low`.
Omitted `low` defaults to zero; omitted `high` defaults to the source length.
An explicit slice bound may extend a slice up to capacity, while an element index must stay below length.
Valid bounds satisfy an ordered non-negative range within the source's allowed limit.
Constant-invalid bounds fail at compile time; invalid dynamic bounds panic at run time.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In `a[low:high]`, `low` is included and `high` is excluded. The result has length `high - low`. This half-open form makes adjacent ranges meet cleanly: `a[:i]` ends exactly where `a[i:]` begins.

In a two-index expression, an omitted low bound defaults to zero and an omitted high bound defaults to the source's current length. Thus `a[:3]` starts at zero, `a[2:]` stops at the current length, and `a[:]` keeps the current visible range.

For a slice, an element access such as `s[i]` requires `i < len(s)`. An explicit slicing bound can extend beyond current length up to capacity. With `s := make([]int, 2, 5)`, `s[3]` panics, but `s = s[:5]` is valid and makes index three accessible.

Reslicing does not initialize a new collection. It reveals elements already in the backing array. With `make([]int, 2, 5)`, those spare elements begin as zero values, but in a subslice they may contain values written through another view. Capacity is a storage boundary, not proof of valid business data.

Bounds known to be impossible as constants are rejected by the compiler. Bounds calculated while the program runs cause a run-time panic when they are negative, out of order, or beyond the permitted limit. Validate external indexes before building the slice expression.

sections.title: Half-open ranges and the reslicing boundary
sections.content:
Go uses half-open slice ranges: the lower position belongs to the result and the upper position does not. This makes the result length a simple subtraction and lets adjacent ranges divide data without a gap or overlap. An empty range is also natural because `a[i:i]` has length zero.

Omitted bounds use the current visible slice. The low bound becomes zero, while the high bound becomes current length. Explicit bounds are more powerful: when slicing a slice, the high bound may extend beyond current length up to capacity. That operation reveals backing-array positions already reserved for the slice.

Indexing remains stricter. Capacity is not a second index range. Before `s = s[:5]`, a slice of length two cannot use `s[3]` even when its capacity is five. After reslicing, the same position becomes part of the visible range. Its value comes from existing storage and may be a zero value or data previously written through an alias.

Compile-time constants let the compiler reject impossible bounds early. Dynamic values are checked at run time and panic when the range is negative, reversed, or too large. Code receiving offsets from a request, file, or user should validate them before slicing so an invalid input becomes a normal error rather than a process panic.

sections.title: Indexing and slicing use different limits
sections.content:
| Operation | Limit that matters | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `s[i]` | `i < len(s)` | Access one currently visible element |
| `s[low:high]` | Ordered bounds with explicit high no greater than `cap(s)` | Create another slice view |
| `s[:high]` | Explicit high no greater than `cap(s)` | Extend or shorten from index zero |
| `s[low:]` | Default high is current `len(s)` | Continue only to the current visible end |

sections.title: Extend a reserved slice before indexing it
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := make([]int, 2, 5)
	s[0], s[1] = 7, 8

	fmt.Println(s, len(s), cap(s))
	s = s[:5]
	s[3] = 9
	fmt.Println(s, len(s), cap(s))
}
```

questions.question: Why can changing one slice also change another slice?
questions.title: Slice aliasing and shared backing arrays in Go
questions.direct_answer: Changing one slice can change another because both slice values may describe overlapping positions in the same underlying array. A subslice copies the descriptor, not the elements. A write changes the shared array element, so every alias reaching that position observes it. Use `copy` or `slices.Clone` when independent storage is required. Append may keep sharing within capacity or move the returned slice to new storage, so append is not a reliable cloning strategy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether aliasing is traced through backing-array positions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating a subslice as an independent copy.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clone when the receiving code needs ownership independent of future mutations.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Assigning or subslicing a slice copies its descriptor, not its elements.
Two slice views can overlap the same positions in one backing array.
A write is visible through every alias whose range reaches that array position.
Use `copy` or `slices.Clone` when the receiver needs independent element storage.
Append may preserve or break sharing depending on capacity, so it does not define ownership.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A slice value describes a range of an underlying array. Creating `middle := all[1:]` makes another slice descriptor; it does not copy the strings or create a new backing array. Both slices can therefore reach some of the same stored positions.

With `all := []string{"red", "green", "blue"}`, `middle[0]` and `all[1]` refer to the same backing-array element. Assigning `middle[0] = "lime"` changes that element, so reading `all[1]` returns `"lime"`.

When the recipient must own a stable snapshot, allocate separate element storage. `snapshot := slices.Clone(all)` is clear in modern Go, while `dst := make([]T, len(src)); copy(dst, src)` expresses the same shallow element copy. Later element assignments no longer cross between those slices.

If an append fits within capacity, it can reuse the same backing array and may overwrite data visible through another slice. If it needs more room, append returns a slice using new storage. The growth strategy is not an ownership contract, so do not use append as an accidental clone.

Share a slice when in-place changes are part of the API. Clone it when callers need independent element storage, and remember that cloning a slice of pointers still copies only the pointer elements. Document whether returned slices may alias internal buffers.

sections.title: Aliasing follows backing-array positions
sections.content:
A slice variable does not own a private element collection. It describes a range of an array, so assigning the slice or creating a subslice normally produces another descriptor for the same storage. To understand a write, translate each relative slice index back to its backing-array position.

Two views only share effects where they can reach the same position. If `middle := all[1:]`, then `middle[0]` is the same stored element as `all[1]`. A write through either view is immediately visible through the other. Their variable names and different lengths do not create ownership boundaries.

Use aliasing deliberately for in-place algorithms and buffer processing. Use `slices.Clone` or `make` plus `copy` when another component needs its own element storage. That copy is still shallow: if each element is a pointer, both slices contain pointers to the same target objects unless those objects are copied too.

Append makes accidental assumptions dangerous. Within capacity it can reuse the shared array; beyond capacity it returns a slice backed by new storage. A small change in starting slice or capacity may therefore change whether an append is observed through an alias. APIs that require isolation should copy explicitly rather than rely on allocation as a side effect.

sections.title: Two slice views reach one stored element
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  A[Backing array - red, green, blue]
  S[all covers positions 0 to 2] --> A
  M[middle covers positions 1 to 2] --> A
  W[middle 0 = lime] --> P[backing position 1 changes]
  P --> S
  P --> M
```
The relative indexes differ, but both views reach backing-array position 1.

sections.title: Observe aliasing, then create a snapshot
sections.content:
```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)

func main() {
	all := []string{"red", "green", "blue"}
	middle := all[1:]
	middle[0] = "lime"

	snapshot := slices.Clone(all)
	snapshot[1] = "gold"

	fmt.Println(all)
	fmt.Println(middle)
	fmt.Println(snapshot)
}
```

questions.question: What is a full slice expression, and why would you use one?
questions.title: Full slice expressions and capacity control in Go
questions.direct_answer: A full slice expression `a[low:high:max]` creates a slice with length `high-low` and capacity `max-low`. The third index places a capacity fence on the new view. If code later appends beyond that limited capacity, append must use different storage instead of reusing adjacent elements in the source array. The full expression is not a copy: elements in its current range still alias the original array. Use a clone when all later element mutation must be independent.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the third index is connected to capacity and append ownership.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling the full slice expression a copy; existing elements are still shared.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a capacity fence for append isolation and a clone for complete mutation isolation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A full slice expression has the form `a[low:high:max]`, with `0 <= low <= high <= max <= cap(a)`.
The result length is `high-low` and its capacity is `max-low`.
The third index limits how far append can reuse the source backing array.
Existing elements still alias the source because the expression does not copy them.
Use a capacity fence for append isolation and a clone for complete element-storage isolation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A full slice expression is written `a[low:high:max]`. Only low may be omitted, and valid bounds satisfy `0 <= low <= high <= max <= cap(a)`. Its length is `high - low`, while its capacity is deliberately limited to `max - low`.

With an ordinary view such as `head := values[:2]`, `head` may inherit capacity covering the rest of `values`. Appending to head can then reuse that array and write into a position that the original slice already exposes.

Using `head := values[:2:2]` gives head length two and capacity two. The next non-empty append exceeds that capacity, so append returns a slice with different storage instead of writing over `values[2]`. The caller must still assign the returned slice.

The three-index expression still points at the same existing elements. Before append, assigning `head[0] = 99` also changes `values[0]`. The capacity fence isolates growth behavior; it does not isolate mutations inside the current shared range.

Use a full slice expression when a helper may append but should not overwrite the source's adjacent elements. Use `slices.Clone` or `copy` when the helper must not change existing source elements either. These solve related but different ownership problems.

sections.title: Capacity fences and append isolation
sections.content:
A full slice expression is written `a[low:high:max]`. It gives the result length `high-low` and capacity `max-low`. Only low may be omitted, and the ordered bounds cannot extend beyond the source capacity.

An ordinary two-index subslice inherits capacity from its source. That spare capacity allows append to place new elements into the same backing array. If another slice already exposes those positions, the append may appear to overwrite unrelated data even though it only followed the capacity available to its receiver.

The third index creates an explicit limit. For `head := values[:2:2]`, low is zero, high is two, and max is two, so both length and capacity are two. Any append that adds an element needs more capacity and returns a slice using different storage. This makes it useful before passing a prefix to code that may append.

A capacity fence is not a snapshot. The elements already inside head still occupy the same array positions as the source, so changing `head[0]` changes `values[0]`. The fence only controls whether growth may reuse positions after the visible range.

Choose the operation from the ownership contract. Use a full slice expression when current elements may remain shared but future append must not consume adjacent source storage. Use `slices.Clone` or an explicit `copy` when even current-element writes must be independent. Keeping those guarantees separate prevents a three-index expression from being mistaken for a copy.

sections.title: Append after a capacity fence
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[values - 10, 20, 30, 40]
  A --> B[head = values 0:2:2]
  B --> C[len 2 and cap 2]
  C -->|append 99| D[new array - 10, 20, 99]
  A --> E[values remains 10, 20, 30, 40]
```
The capacity fence makes the append allocate instead of reusing the source's third position.

sections.title: Fence a subslice before handing it to append
sections.content:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	values := []int{10, 20, 30, 40}
	head := values[:2:2]

	head[0] = 11
	fmt.Println("shared current element:", values)

	head = append(head, 99)
	fmt.Println("grown head:", head)
	fmt.Println("original values:", values)
}
```
